blocks.text: 1. Dot Product

blocks.alt: Vector A is multiplied and summed to produce a score

blocks.text: Dot product keeps magnitude in the comparison, giving the second of the three main candidates its own full treatment.
It multiplies matching positions of two vectors together and sums the results, a magnitude sensitive metric.
2. Keeping Magnitude In Play

blocks.alt: Dot product is compared against cosine, which ignores magnitude

blocks.text: As covered in Cosine Similarity, cosine similarity stripped magnitude out entirely; dot product instead keeps it in play.
A longer vector can produce a larger dot product even at the same angle.
3. The Formula Itself
The dot product formula multiplies each matching pair of dimensions and adds every product together.
No division step happens afterward, unlike cosine similarity.
4. Unbounded Score Range

blocks.alt: A dot product score is compared against a cosine score bounded from -1 to 1

blocks.text: Unlike the fixed score range covered in Cosine Similarity, dot product has no fixed minimum or maximum value.
The resulting score can grow arbitrarily large or small depending on vector magnitude.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Score range"],"rows":[["Cosine similarity","Fixed, between negative one and positive one"],["Dot product","Unbounded, depends on vector magnitude"]]}

blocks.text: 5. When Dot Product Equals Cosine

blocks.alt: Normalized vectors make dot product equal cosine

blocks.text: As covered under the relationship to dot product in Cosine Similarity, once vectors are normalized to unit length, dot product equals cosine similarity exactly.
That equivalence is why so many systems normalize before using dot product.
6. Faster Than Cosine In Practice

blocks.alt: Dot product skips normalization while cosine needs an extra normalization step

blocks.text: As with the computational efficiency covered in Cosine Similarity, dot product skips the magnitude division step entirely.
This makes it one of the fastest similarity computations available on normalized vectors.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Precomputing normalized vectors once during ingestion lets every later query use plain dot product instead of full cosine similarity, saving the division step on every single comparison.

blocks.text: 7. When Magnitude Carries Real Signal
Some embedding models deliberately encode confidence or importance into a vector's magnitude.
In those specific cases, dot product captures information that cosine similarity would discard.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Blindly normalizing vectors before comparison throws away magnitude information. If a specific embedding model relies on magnitude to encode meaning, normalizing it first destroys that signal.

blocks.text: 8. Hardware Acceleration For Dot Product

blocks.alt: Dot product benefits from GPU and SIMD acceleration

blocks.text: Modern hardware is heavily optimized for exactly this kind of multiply and sum operation.
Vector databases, covered in a later module, often default to dot product for raw performance reasons.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Dot Product Is The Right Metric

blocks.alt: Magnitude carrying real meaning points toward using dot product

blocks.text: Already normalized vectors needing maximum speed favor dot product.
Comparing vectors of meaningfully different magnitude, on the other hand, favors cosine similarity, as covered in Cosine Similarity.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using raw dot product to compare vectors of very different magnitude without normalizing first.
Assuming dot product and cosine similarity always produce the same ranking on unnormalized vectors.
Normalizing vectors by default even when a model deliberately encodes signal in magnitude.
Ignoring the unbounded score range, making raw dot product scores hard to interpret directly.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Dot product multiplies matching positions of two vectors together and sums the results.
Unlike cosine similarity, it keeps vector magnitude in the comparison rather than stripping it out.
The formula has no division step, making it simpler and cheaper than cosine similarity.
Its score range is unbounded, unlike cosine similarity's fixed range between negative one and one.
Dot product equals cosine similarity exactly once both vectors are normalized to unit length.
Skipping the division step makes dot product one of the fastest similarity computations available.
Some models deliberately encode signal in magnitude, where dot product captures more information.
Modern hardware is heavily optimized for dot product, making it a common default in vector databases.
